The R FAQ entry for the question "Where have all the methods gone?" explains why so many S3 methods are hidden: they are in namespaces, which has the advantage that they cannot be called inadvertently with arguments of the wrong class, and the disadvantage that they are harder to view. getS3method("[", "terms") is the FAQ’s example of how to see one, and pkg:::name is the way to see an unexported function; the FAQ adds that the latter should not be used in your own code (R FAQ 7.26: Where have all the methods gone?).

Where a method has to be to be found

The lookup rule from the dispatch section has a consequence that surprises people who define methods inside functions: a method is found if it is visible in the environment of the call to the generic, or if it is registered. Both are true of methods defined at top level or in a package namespace; neither is true of a method defined inside a function body when the generic is called from somewhere else.

describe <- function(x, ...) {
  UseMethod("describe")
}
describe.default <- function(x, ...) "default method"
x <- structure(1, class = "foo")

# A method defined inside a function is found only by calls made from there.
direct <- function(x) {
  describe.foo <- function(x, ...) "local method" # nolint: object_usage_linter.
  describe(x)
}
direct(x)
#> [1] "local method"

# vapply() calls describe() from its own frame, so the local method is lost.
via_vapply <- function(x) {
  describe.foo <- function(x, ...) "local method" # nolint: object_usage_linter.
  vapply(list(x), describe, character(1L))
}
via_vapply(x)
#> [1] "default method"

# A helper defined elsewhere calls the generic from its own environment.
helper <- function(x) {
  describe(x)
}
via_helper <- function(x) {
  describe.foo <- function(x, ...) "local method" # nolint: object_usage_linter.
  helper(x)
}
via_helper(x)
#> [1] "default method"

# The same happens with local() at top level.
local({
  describe.foo <- function(x, ...) "method inside local()"
  print(describe(x))
})
#> [1] "method inside local()"
describe(x)
#> [1] "default method"

# Registering the method puts it where every call to the generic finds it.
.S3method("describe", "foo", function(x, ...) "registered method")
describe(x)
#> [1] "registered method"
via_vapply(x)
#> [1] "registered method"
exists("describe.foo")
#> [1] FALSE
methods(describe)
#> [1] describe.default describe.foo*
#> see '?methods' for accessing help and source code
body(getS3method("describe", "foo"))
#> [1] "registered method"

# A visible method in the calling environment wins over a registered one.
describe.foo <- function(x, ...) "method in the global environment"
describe(x)
#> [1] "method in the global environment"
rm(describe.foo)
describe(x)
#> [1] "registered method"

Source: R documentation: UseMethod

The first call works: describe(x) is called inside direct(), so describe.foo is visible in its calling environment. When the same generic is called from vapply() the calling environment is the vapply frame, so the local method is not found and the default answers; the same happens when the call is made in a helper function defined elsewhere. local() at top level behaves like a function body: found inside, lost outside. After .S3method("describe", "foo", ...) registers a method, it is found everywhere, even from inside vapply(), but exists("describe.foo") is FALSE, because registration does not create a variable, and methods(describe) shows describe.foo* with the asterisk for "not visible". Finally a method visible in the global environment (the calling environment) beats a registered method for the same class, which is a consequence of the search order. When scripts use vapply() or lapply() over objects with local methods, define the methods at top level or register them.

Registering methods

A package must not rely on the global environment: the standard S3 lookup might fail to find methods defined in a package that is imported but not attached, so the methods need to be registered. In the package’s NAMESPACE file the directive is S3method(generic, class). It makes print.book available for dispatch without exporting the function (Writing R Extensions: Registering S3 methods):

export(book, shelf)
S3method(print, book)
S3method(format, book)
S3method(summary, book)
S3method(print, summary.book)
S3method("[", shelf)
S3method("[[<-", shelf)
S3method(c, shelf)
S3method(print, shelf, print_shelf)

Source: Writing R Extensions: Registering S3 methods

The directive takes the generic and the class; the third optional argument is the function to use as the method, for example S3method(print, shelf, print_shelf) when the function is not called print.shelf. Function and class names may be quoted, and reserved words and non-standard names such as [<- must be quoted. The generic must be visible to the package: since print is defined in base it needs no import, but for a generic from another package it must be imported with importFrom(). Export the generics, constructors and helpers, but export methods only through S3method(), not through export() or a wide exportPattern(), which would also export internal helpers. "Writing R Extensions" cautions that broad patterns are not recommended for production code (Writing R Extensions: Specifying imports and exports).

There are two more cases. For a method on a generic from a package you do not want to load until needed (a package in Suggests, for example), R 3.6.0 added delayed registration (listed in the R NEWS: Changes in R 3.6.0 among the changes to namespaces): S3method(pkg::gen, cls) registers gen.cls as a method for the generic gen of package pkg only when the namespace of pkg is loaded. The manual’s example wraps the directive in an if (getRversion() >= "3.6.0") condition for packages that must also install on older R versions. And for scripts, which have no NAMESPACE, R 4.0.0 added .S3method(generic, class, method) (listed as a new function in the 4.0.0 NEWS): the help page says that it should only be used in R scripts, and that package code should use the S3method directive. registerS3method(genname, class, method, envir) is the function that .S3method() calls (with envir set to the calling environment, so that the generic is searched first where .S3method() was called); it is documented with the namespace internals (R documentation: .S3method, R documentation: registerS3method).

Letting roxygen2 write the directives

Few packages write the NAMESPACE by hand: roxygen2 generates it from comments. The tag @export on a function that is recognisably a method (a name of the form generic.class where generic is a generic visible to the package) produces S3method(generic, class); on any other function it produces export(). A method for a generic from another package that should be registered lazily uses @exportS3Method pkg::gen, which produces the delayed-registration directive. The script below builds a throwaway package in a temporary directory, runs roxygen2::roxygenise() (roxygen2 8.1.1) and prints what it wrote:

# Build a throwaway package and let roxygen2 write its NAMESPACE.
pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "shelfmate")
dir.create(file.path(pkg, "R"), recursive = TRUE)

writeLines(c(
  "Package: shelfmate",
  "Title: Books on a Shelf",
  "Version: 0.0.1",
  "Description: The book class of the shelf scenario.",
  "License: MIT",
  "Encoding: UTF-8"
), file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION"))

writeLines(c(
  "#' Create a book",
  "#' @param title The title.",
  "#' @return A book.",
  "#' @export",
  "book <- function(title) {",
  "  structure(list(title = title), class = \"book\")",
  "}",
  "",
  "#' Print a book",
  "#' @param x A book.",
  "#' @param ... Not used.",
  "#' @export",
  "print.book <- function(x, ...) {",
  "  cat(\"<book>\", x$title, \"\\n\")",
  "  invisible(x)",
  "}",
  "",
  "#' Subset a shelf",
  "#' @param x A shelf.",
  "#' @param i An index.",
  "#' @param ... Not used.",
  "#' @export",
  "`[.shelf` <- function(x, i, ...) {",
  "  structure(NextMethod(), class = \"shelf\")",
  "}",
  "",
  "#' Tidy a book",
  "#' @param x A book.",
  "#' @param ... Not used.",
  "#' @exportS3Method generics::tidy",
  "tidy.book <- function(x, ...) {",
  "  data.frame(title = x$title)",
  "}",
  "",
  "#' A helper that is not a method",
  "#' @param x Anything.",
  "#' @keywords internal",
  "#' @noRd",
  "print_helper <- function(x) x"
), file.path(pkg, "R", "book.R"))

invisible(capture.output(
  roxygen2::roxygenise(pkg),
  type = "message"
))

cat(readLines(file.path(pkg, "NAMESPACE")), sep = "\n")
#> # Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand
#>
#> S3method("[",shelf)
#> S3method(generics::tidy,book)
#> S3method(print,book)
#> export(book)
desc <- read.dcf(file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION"))
colnames(desc)
#> [1] "Package"                 "Title"
#> [3] "Version"                 "Description"
#> [5] "License"                 "Encoding"
#> [7] "Config/roxygen2/version"
unname(desc[1L, "Config/roxygen2/version"])
#> [1] "8.1.1"
list.files(file.path(pkg, "man"))
#> [1] "book.Rd"       "print.book.Rd" "sub-.shelf.Rd" "tidy.book.Rd"

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Managing imports and exports

The NAMESPACE has the three kinds of directive: export(book) for the helper, S3method(print,book) for a method found by name, and S3method("[",shelf) for a method of an internal generic (note that the quotes are generated for the non-standard name). @exportS3Method generics::tidy generated S3method(generics::tidy,book), the delayed-registration form of the previous paragraph, for a generic that lives in another package. Under roxygen2 8.x the version is recorded in the Config/roxygen2/version field of DESCRIPTION (here 8.1.1), not in the older note-style field that many tutorials still show. The helper tagged @noRd produced no Rd file and no directive. The same NAMESPACE generated by hand would have to be kept in step with the code; regenerating it after each change (devtools::document()) is the habit that prevents a method that works in load_all() and is not found in the installed package. Packages, namespaces and the NAMESPACE file are covered in Packages, Libraries and Namespaces, package creation in Creating Packages, and the documentation tags in Documentation with Rd, roxygen2 and Vignettes.

A method also needs documentation, but the manual lets it be brief: in the Rd usage section of the generic’s page, S3 methods are written with the \method{generic}{class}(arguments) macro, which keeps the usage in step with the generic’s arguments and lets R CMD check compare them (Writing R Extensions: Documenting functions). Roxygen2 writes the macro for you.

Inheritance with class vectors

S3 inheritance is nothing more than a class vector with more than one element and methods that cooperate through NextMethod(). The Language Definition states it in two sentences: the class attribute can have several elements, and the first inheritance is mainly handled through NextMethod(), which determines the method currently being evaluated, finds the next class from the class attribute and proceeds (R-lang: Inheritance). A subclass is therefore an object whose class vector starts with the subclass name and continues with the parent’s class vector, and the parent’s constructor, validator and methods are reused where they fit.

An audiobook is a book with a narrator and a duration in minutes. Its constructor takes a finished book, adds two fields and prepends the new class to the book’s own class vector; its validator calls the parent’s validator first (which accepts the extra fields, because validate_book() checks that every field has length 1 rather than the exact list of names) and then checks its own rule; and its helper builds the book with book(), so every parent rule applies:

source("scenario.R")

# A subclass: constructor, validator and helper, reusing the parent's pieces.
new_audiobook <- function(book, narrator = character(), minutes = integer()) {
  stopifnot(
    inherits(book, "book"),
    is.character(narrator),
    is.integer(minutes)
  )
  structure(
    c(unclass(book), list(narrator = narrator, minutes = minutes)),
    class = c("audiobook", class(book))
  )
}

validate_audiobook <- function(x) {
  validate_book(x) # nolint: object_usage_linter.
  if (!is.na(x$minutes) && x$minutes <= 0L) {
    stop("minutes must be positive", call. = FALSE)
  }
  x
}

audiobook <- function(title, ..., narrator = NA_character_,
                      minutes = NA_integer_) {
  validate_audiobook(
    new_audiobook(
      book(title, ...), # nolint: object_usage_linter.
      trimws(narrator),
      as.integer(minutes)
    )
  )
}

Source: R documentation: UseMethod

Three design decisions are worth stating. The subclass constructor is built from a book, not from the six raw fields, so there is one place that knows how to build a book. The class vector is created with class = c("audiobook", class(book)) rather than a literal c("audiobook", "book"), so a further subclass (c("audiobook", "book") becoming c("radio_drama", "audiobook", "book")) keeps working. And the validator relies on the parent’s validator instead of repeating its rules, so a change to the book rules reaches every subclass.

The methods of the subclass override or extend the parent’s. format.audiobook() takes the parent’s description and appends the narrator; summary.audiobook() takes the parent’s summary and adds the number of minutes; print.summary.audiobook() lets the parent’s method print what it knows and then adds its own line. Each begins or ends with NextMethod(), so the parent’s code is not repeated:

# Methods: format() extends the parent's result with NextMethod().
format.audiobook <- function(x, ...) {
  paste0(NextMethod(), ", read by ", x$narrator)
}

summary.audiobook <- function(object, ...) {
  out <- NextMethod()
  out$minutes <- object$minutes
  class(out) <- c("summary.audiobook", class(out))
  out
}

print.summary.audiobook <- function(x, ...) {
  NextMethod()
  cat("Minutes:", x$minutes, "\n")
  invisible(x)
}

Source: R documentation: UseMethod

An audiobook needs no print method of its own. The call print(a) found print.book (the first element of the class vector with a print method), which called format(x), and that dispatched again, this time to format.audiobook: a method in the parent’s code is extended by overriding one generic that it calls. This late binding, where the parent’s print behaviour changes because the subclass changed format, is what makes the pattern of printing by calling format() worthwhile.

a <- audiobook(
  "Dune", "Frank Herbert", "978-0-306-40615-7", 1965, "Classic", 412,
  narrator = "Simon Vance", minutes = 1260
)
class(a)
#> [1] "audiobook" "book"
inherits(a, "book")
#> [1] TRUE
inherits(a, c("book", "audiobook", "podcast"), which = TRUE)
#> [1] 2 1 0
names(a)
#> [1] "title"    "author"   "isbn"     "year"     "genre"    "pages"    "narrator"
#> [8] "minutes"

# print.book() is inherited; it calls format(), which finds format.audiobook().
a
#> <book> Dune (Frank Herbert, 1965), read by Simon Vance
format(a)
#> [1] "Dune (Frank Herbert, 1965), read by Simon Vance"
summary(a)
#> Book: Dune
#> ISBN known: TRUE
#> Pages: 412
#> Minutes: 1260
class(summary(a))
#> [1] "summary.audiobook" "summary.book"

# Which method would be used? Walk the class vector like UseMethod() does.
method_for <- function(generic, x) {
  for (cl in c(class(x), "default")) {
    if (!is.null(utils::getS3method(generic, cl, optional = TRUE))) {
      return(paste(generic, cl, sep = "."))
    }
  }
  NA_character_
}
generics <- c("print", "format", "summary", "toString")
vapply(generics, method_for, character(1L), x = a)
#>               print              format             summary            toString
#>        "print.book"  "format.audiobook" "summary.audiobook"  "toString.default"

# The order of the class vector is the order of the search.
reordered <- a
class(reordered) <- c("book", "audiobook")
format(reordered)
#> [1] "Dune (Frank Herbert, 1965)"
vapply(generics, method_for, character(1L), x = reordered)
#>              print             format            summary           toString
#>       "print.book"      "format.book"     "summary.book" "toString.default"

# The validators chain too.
tryCatch(audiobook("Dune", minutes = 0L), error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "minutes must be positive"
tryCatch(audiobook("", minutes = 10L), error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "a book needs a title"

Source: R documentation: class

inherits(a, "book") is TRUE for the subclass, and with which = TRUE it returns the positions 2 1 0 of "book", "audiobook" and "podcast" in the class vector of a (zero when the class is not there). method_for() walks the class vector the way UseMethod() does and reports the method that would be chosen (it ignores implicit classes and registered methods that getS3method() does not find from its own frame, so it is a teaching device, not a debugging tool); print.book, format.audiobook, summary.audiobook and toString.default are the answers for a. Reversing the class vector with class(reordered) <- c("book", "audiobook") changes the answers: the same object now uses format.book first, and nothing complained, because nothing in S3 verifies that the order makes sense. The order of the class vector is the order of the search, and the specific class must come first. The two tryCatch() calls at the end show the validators chained: the audiobook’s own rule fires for zero minutes, and the book’s rule for an empty title.

S3 inheritance has no way to say that a class is abstract, no multiple dispatch, and no check that a subclass keeps the parent’s promises: the parent’s methods trust that the object has the parent’s fields. Where a class system needs those guarantees, the formal systems exist: S4 Classes and Methods adds declared slots, validity, virtual classes and multiple dispatch, and The S7 Object System is the successor under development.

Testing for a class

The class vector can have several elements, so tests that treat class(x) as a single string are wrong in general, and they have become visibly wrong in two places in recent R versions. First, class(matrix(1:4, 2)) has length two since R 4.0.0, and the 4.0.0 NEWS points out that code which assumes the class of a matrix has length one is invalid. Second, R 4.2.0 turned the warning for an if or while condition of length greater than one into an error (R NEWS: Changes in R 4.2.0), so the common test if (class(x) == "book") stops as soon as x has two classes. The same 4.2.0 NEWS also records that the result of ks.test() now has class c("ks.test", "htest") and tells package authors who test the class to use inherits() and not ==.

source("scenario.R")
msg <- function(expr) {
  tryCatch(expr, error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
}

plain <- book("Dune")
sub <- structure(c(unclass(plain), list(narrator = "N")),
  class = c("audiobook", "book")
)

# == on the class works for a one-element class vector only.
class(plain) == "book"
#> [1] TRUE
class(sub) == "book"
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE
msg(if (class(sub) == "book") "a book")
#> [1] "the condition has length > 1"

# inherits() answers the right question: is it a book, possibly a subclass?
inherits(plain, "book")
#> [1] TRUE
inherits(sub, "book")
#> [1] TRUE
inherits(sub, "audiobook")
#> [1] TRUE
inherits(plain, "audiobook")
#> [1] FALSE

# which = TRUE gives the position in the class vector, 0 when absent.
inherits(sub, c("audiobook", "book", "podcast"), which = TRUE)
#> [1] 1 2 0

# isa() requires all the classes, in any order.
isa(sub, "book")
#> [1] TRUE
isa(sub, c("book", "audiobook"))
#> [1] TRUE
isa(plain, c("book", "audiobook"))
#> [1] FALSE

# identical() on the class vector is the strict test: exactly this class.
identical(class(plain), "book")
#> [1] TRUE
identical(class(sub), "book")
#> [1] FALSE

# class<- accepts any character vector: nothing checks that it makes sense.
broken <- structure(list(), class = "book")
inherits(broken, "book")
#> [1] TRUE
msg(validate_book(broken))
#> [1] "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed"
msg(format(broken))
#> [1] "argument is of length zero"

Source: R documentation: class

class(sub) == "book" returned FALSE TRUE for an object with two classes, and if (class(sub) == "book") stopped with the condition has length > 1. The reliable tests are:

  • inherits(x, "book") for "is it a book, possibly a subclass?", and inherits(x, c("a", "b"), which = TRUE) when the position matters;

  • isa(x, c("book", "audiobook")) when all the classes must be present (any order);

  • identical(class(x), "book") when the object must be exactly a book and not a subclass;

  • is.object(x) for "does it have a class attribute at all?".

Since R 4.3.0, inherits(x, what) accepts values for what that are not plain character vectors: a new generic, nameOfClass(), is called to resolve the class name, so that alternative object systems can plug into inherits() (R NEWS: Changes in R 4.3.0). The last lines of the script show the other side of the coin: nothing prevents structure(list(), class = "book"), and inherits() says TRUE for an object that has none of a book’s fields; the validator, run on it, fails with a message about missing values, and format() fails inside the method. A class test checks the label, not the contents.

Pitfalls

Where have all the methods gone?

R FAQ 7.26 explains why S3 methods are often not visible: many are hidden in namespaces, which has the advantage that they cannot be called inadvertently with arguments of the wrong class. The tools shown above (getS3method(), getAnywhere(), methods()) retrieve them, and pkg:::name reads an unexported function but should not be used in your own code. The other half of the question, "why is my method not called?", has a short checklist:

  • the method is defined where the call to the generic cannot see it (inside a function, in local(), in an environment that the generic’s caller does not have) and is not registered: see the vapply() example in the previous section;

  • the method is in a package namespace and is not registered: it is only found when the package is attached. The fix is the S3method() directive in NAMESPACE, or @export with roxygen2;

  • the method name is wrong: print.Book is not print.book (class names are case sensitive), or the class vector was reordered;

  • the class was lost on the way: [, c(), unlist(), lapply() results, rbind() and arithmetic often return plain vectors or lists, because the internal defaults drop the class (see the shelf section);

  • the arguments do not match the generic: unused argument appears when the generic passes something the method does not accept;

  • a function with a method-like name is called instead (next subsection).

Printing and the visible value

Automatic printing, which is what calls the print method, happens only for a visible value at the top level, as R FAQ 7.16 explains in the context of source(). Inside a for loop, inside a function whose value is not returned to the top level, or in a script run with source() without echo or print.eval, nothing is printed unless the code calls print() itself.

source("scenario.R")
pair <- list(book("First", year = 1990), book("Second", year = 2001))

# Only a visible value at top level is printed, by calling print() on it.
pair[[1]]
#> <book> First (NA, 1990)
invisible(pair[[1]])
(invisible(pair[[1]]))
#> <book> First (NA, 1990)

# Inside a loop, or a function that is not at the end of the line, nothing is
# printed automatically: call print() yourself.
for (b in pair) {
  b
}
for (b in pair) {
  print(b)
}
#> <book> First (NA, 1990)
#> <book> Second (NA, 2001)
show_all <- function(items) {
  for (b in items) {
    print(b)
  }
  invisible(items)
}
show_all(pair)
#> <book> First (NA, 1990)
#> <book> Second (NA, 2001)
res <- show_all(pair)
#> <book> First (NA, 1990)
#> <book> Second (NA, 2001)
length(res)
#> [1] 2

# print() returns its argument invisibly, which is what makes this work.
x <- print(pair[[2]])
#> <book> Second (NA, 2001)
identical(x, pair[[2]])
#> [1] TRUE

# A function that ends with an assignment returns its value invisibly too.
f <- function(b) {
  out <- format(b) # nolint: object_usage_linter.
}
f(pair[[1]])
(f(pair[[1]]))
#> [1] "First (NA, 1990)"

# source() prints top-level values only with echo or print.eval.
source(exprs = quote(pair[[1]]))
source(exprs = quote(pair[[1]]), print.eval = TRUE)
#> <book> First (NA, 1990)

Source: R FAQ 7.16: Why is the output not printed when I source() a file?

The first expression printed the book because it was a visible value at the top level; the two forms with invisible() show that visibility, not the value, decides. The for (b in pair) b loop printed nothing at all, while print(b) printed both books. show_all() returns its argument invisibly, so calling it at top level prints once per print() inside the loop and does not print the list again; that is the idiom used by print methods (do the printing, return invisible(x)). A function whose last expression is an assignment (f()) also returns invisibly, so f(pair[[1]]) shows nothing, and wrapping the call in parentheses forces printing. source() prints top-level values only with echo = TRUE or print.eval = TRUE, which is why scripts that "work" in the console print nothing under Rscript or source(): a bare b line is not a statement that prints. See Idioms and Common Pitfalls for more of these habits.

Partial matching with $ on list-based objects

An S3 object built on a list is read with $, and $ on a list matches names partially. A misspelt or abbreviated field name silently returns the value of a field whose name starts with the typed text:

source("scenario.R")
b <- book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", year = 1965, pages = 412)

# $ on a list matches names partially: a misspelt field still "works".
b$pag
#> [1] 412
b$yea
#> [1] 1965
b$y
#> [1] 1965
b$au
#> [1] "Frank Herbert"

# A field that does not exist is NULL, not an error.
b$publisher
#> NULL
is.null(b$pub)
#> [1] TRUE

# [[ matches exactly unless asked otherwise.
b[["pag"]]
#> NULL
b[["pag", exact = FALSE]]
#> [1] 412

# The option warnPartialMatchDollar reports every partial match.
op <- options(warnPartialMatchDollar = TRUE)
withCallingHandlers(
  b$pag,
  warning = \(w) {
    cat("warning:", conditionMessage(w), "\n")
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
#> warning: partial match of 'pag' to 'pages'
#> [1] 412
options(op)

# Two candidates are ambiguous and give NULL.
ambiguous <- structure(list(year = 1965L, yearly = 12L), class = "book")
ambiguous$yea
#> NULL
ambiguous$year
#> [1] 1965

Source: R documentation: Extract

b$pag returned the pages, b$yea the year, b$y the year again (the only field starting with y), and b$au the author; a name that matches nothing, b$publisher, is NULL, not an error, which means a typo can silently turn a number into NULL and then into a vector of length zero. [[ is exact unless asked with exact = FALSE. The option warnPartialMatchDollar makes every partial match on a $ warn: partial match of 'pag' to 'pages'. When two names match, the result is NULL (the last lines: year and yearly both start with yea). Use [[ with the full name in functions that matter, or turn the option on in tests; Subsetting and Indexing explains the rules for $ and [[ in general.

Comparing, printing the raw list and looking inside

A classed list is still a list, and the list tools see through the class. identical() compares the class attribute as well as the data, so a book and its unclass() copy are not identical, and all.equal() describes the first difference it finds. The == operator has no book method, so it falls to the default for lists and stops with comparison of these types is not implemented; to compare books by value, compare unclass() copies, define a method for Ops (S3 Group Generics and Operator Overloading) or compare chosen fields. To see an object without the method getting in the way, use unclass(), str(), attributes() or print.default():

source("scenario.R")
a <- book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", year = 1965)
b <- book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", year = 1965)
c2 <- book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", year = 1966)

# identical() and all.equal() compare the class attribute as well as the data.
identical(a, b)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(a, c2)
#> [1] FALSE
all.equal(a, b)
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(a, c2)
#> [1] "Component “year”: Mean relative difference: 0.0005089059"
identical(a, unclass(a))
#> [1] FALSE
all.equal(unclass(a), unclass(c2))
#> [1] "Component “year”: Mean relative difference: 0.0005089059"
identical(unclass(a), unclass(b))
#> [1] TRUE

# == is not defined for a book: the default method works on the list.
tryCatch(a == b, error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "comparison of these types is not implemented"

# Seeing inside an object: unclass(), str(), attributes() and names().
str(unclass(a))
#> List of 6
#>  $ title : chr "Dune"
#>  $ author: chr "Frank Herbert"
#>  $ isbn  : chr NA
#>  $ year  : int 1965
#>  $ genre : chr NA
#>  $ pages : int NA
attributes(a)
#> $names
#> [1] "title"  "author" "isbn"   "year"   "genre"  "pages"
#>
#> $class
#> [1] "book"
#>
names(a)
#> [1] "title"  "author" "isbn"   "year"   "genre"  "pages"
mode(a)
#> [1] "list"
typeof(a)
#> [1] "list"
is.list(a)
#> [1] TRUE
length(a)
#> [1] 6

# The same object with the print method bypassed.
print(unclass(a)[c("title", "year")])
#> $title
#> [1] "Dune"
#>
#> $year
#> [1] 1965
#>
print.default(a)
#> $title
#> [1] "Dune"
#>
#> $author
#> [1] "Frank Herbert"
#>
#> $isbn
#> [1] NA
#>
#> $year
#> [1] 1965
#>
#> $genre
#> [1] NA
#>
#> $pages
#> [1] NA
#>
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "book"

Source: R documentation: identical

all.equal(a, c2) pointed at the differing component with Component “year”: Mean relative difference: 0.0005089059, and all.equal(unclass(a), unclass(c2)) gave the same message without the class attribute. str(unclass(a)) shows the six fields, attributes(a) shows names and class and nothing else, and print.default(a) prints the raw list, ending with attr(,"class") so that the class is visible. print(unclass(a)[c("title", "year")]) prints selected fields without the method. The print.default() call is also how a method delegates to the built-in printing; NextMethod() does the same job inside a print method.

Naming clashes: when a function is a method by accident

Any function named generic.class is a method, whether or not that was intended. A plain helper such as describe.list, written to describe a list of books, becomes the method for every plain list in the session, because the implicit class of a list is "list":

msg <- function(expr) {
  tryCatch(expr, error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
}

# A name of the form generic.class is a method, whatever the author meant.
describe <- function(x, ...) {
  UseMethod("describe")
}
describe.default <- function(x, ...) "default"

# Meant as a helper "to describe a list of books" ...
describe.list <- function(x, ...) {
  paste(length(x), "items")
}
# ... but every plain list now dispatches to it.
describe(list(1, 2, 3))
#> [1] "3 items"
describe(list())
#> [1] "0 items"
describe(1:3)
#> [1] "default"

# A data frame has a class attribute, so the implicit class "list" is never
# tried for it: the default method answers until it gets a method of its own.
describe(data.frame(a = 1))
#> [1] "default"
describe.data.frame <- function(x, ...) "a data frame"
describe(data.frame(a = 1))
#> [1] "a data frame"

# Base R has two well-known near-misses: t.test() is not a method of t() for
# class "test", and sort.list() is not a method of sort() for lists.
utils::isS3stdGeneric(t)
#>    t
#> TRUE
utils::isS3method("t.test")
#> [1] FALSE
utils::isS3method("sort.list")
#> [1] FALSE
getS3method("t", "test", optional = TRUE)
#> NULL
is.null(getS3method("sort", "list", optional = TRUE))
#> [1] TRUE
msg(sort(list(2, 1)))
#> [1] "'x' must be atomic"

Source: An Introduction to R: Classes, generic functions and object orientation

describe(list(1, 2, 3)) called the helper, which the author meant for something else. A data frame is not captured by it, because it has a class attribute and the implicit class "list" is tried only for objects without one; it would be captured once a method for data.frame exists, which is what the script shows next. Base R has two well-known near-misses, t.test() (is it the t() method for class test?) and sort.list() (is it the sort() method for lists?). Neither is a method: utils::isS3method() says FALSE for both, getS3method("t", "test", optional = TRUE) is NULL and sort(list(2, 1)) reports an error from the default method rather than from sort.list(). The NEWS for R 4.3.3 records one of these: getS3method("t", "test") no longer finds t.test(). The rule that follows is the one the manuals give: do not name functions in the style generic.class unless they are meant to be methods. Use describe_list(), book_describe() or describe_books(), and when you need a name that contains dots, check the prefix against the list of generics (methods() and utils::isS3stdGeneric()).

Version notes

Version Change Where it matters

R 3.5.0

S3 method lookup searches the namespace registry after the top level environment of the calling environment

the lookup order of a call to a generic

R 3.6.0

S3method() directives in NAMESPACE can do delayed registration, S3method(pkg::gen, cls)

methods for generics from packages in Suggests

R 4.0.0

.S3method() registers methods in scripts; .class2() returns the full vector used for dispatch; matrices also inherit from "array", and S3 methods for class "array" are dispatched for matrices

scripts without a NAMESPACE; debugging dispatch; code that assumed class(m) has length one

R 4.2.0

if and while conditions of length greater than one are an error; UseMethod() no longer crashes when it cannot dispatch on an object with a very long class vector (4.2.3)

if (class(x) == "book") for an object with several classes

R 4.3.0

inherits(x, what) accepts a non-character what, resolved by the new generic nameOfClass(); chooseOpsMethod() for Ops conflicts

alternative object systems such as S7

R 4.3.3

getS3method("t", "test") no longer finds t.test()

naming clashes in the lookup helpers

R 4.4.0

UseMethod() no longer forwards local variables of the generic into the method; methods() and .S3methods() gain all.names

methods that read variables set by the generic

R 4.6.0

str() of a list-like object whose class has an str() method that calls NextMethod() no longer prints a "List of" header from the default method

printing of classed lists

Source: R NEWS: Changes in R 4.0.0, 4.2.0, 4.2.3, 4.3.0, 4.3.3, 4.4.0 and 4.6.0

The R 3.5.0 and 3.6.0 items are in the R NEWS for the 3.x series. All the examples on this page were run on R 4.6.1. Behaviour that changed in 4.4.0 (the local variables) and 4.0.0 (the matrix class) is the part most likely to matter in old code; inherits(which = TRUE) is documented on the class help page and is older than the NEWS files kept for the 3.x series, so no introduction version is stated for it.

Where older tutorials differ

Much of what is written about S3 predates the constructor and validator habit, the invisible(x) convention and the registration mechanism. Following that older material produces classes that work interactively and fail when they are put in a package, or when somebody passes them a slightly different input:

msg <- function(expr) {
  tryCatch(expr, error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
}

# The style of many older tutorials: a bare list, a class assignment, no checks.
b <- list(title = "Dune", year = "nineteen sixty-five", pages = 1:3)
class(b) <- "oldbook"
attr(b, "class")
#> [1] "oldbook"
inherits(b, "oldbook")
#> [1] TRUE

# A print method without ... and without invisible(x).
print.oldbook <- function(x) {
  cat("<oldbook>", x$title, "\n")
}
b
#> <oldbook> Dune
msg(print(b, digits = 3))
#> [1] "unused argument (digits = 3)"
y <- print(b)
#> <oldbook> Dune
is.null(y)
#> [1] TRUE
msg(b |> print() |> format())
#> <oldbook> Dune
#> [1] "NULL"

# The modern shape of the same method.
print.oldbook <- function(x, ...) {
  cat("<oldbook>", x$title, "\n")
  invisible(x)
}
y <- print(b, digits = 3)
#> <oldbook> Dune
identical(y, b)
#> [1] TRUE

# Nothing stopped the nonsense: wrong types, wrong lengths, a missing title.
str(unclass(b))
#> List of 3
#>  $ title: chr "Dune"
#>  $ year : chr "nineteen sixty-five"
#>  $ pages: int [1:3] 1 2 3
bad <- structure(list(), class = "oldbook")
msg(print(bad))
#> <oldbook>

Source: R documentation: print

The script shows several things at once. The class was assigned to a bare list with class(b) <- "oldbook", and attr(b, "class") reads it back: both work, but nothing was checked, so the year is a string and the pages are an integer vector of length three, and a completely empty structure(list(), class = "oldbook") prints <oldbook> with no title and no complaint. The old print.oldbook(x) has no ..., so print(b, digits = 3) stops with unused argument (digits = 3), and it ends with cat(), so it returns NULL: y <- print(b) gives NULL and a pipeline such as b |> print() |> format() ends up formatting NULL. The modern version has the generic’s arguments and ends with invisible(x).

Older tutorials Today Why

class(x) <- "book" on a bare list, no constructor

A constructor with structure(), a validator and a helper function

nothing else checks that an object has the fields its methods expect (R-lang: "Classes")

attr(x, "class") <- "book" or attributes(x) <- list(class = ...)

structure(..., class = ...) in the constructor, class(x) <- ... elsewhere; oldClass() when only the attribute is wanted

the replacement functions say what they do, and oldClass() never reports an implicit class

print.book <- function(x) cat(...)

print.book <- function(x, ...) that ends with invisible(x)

the generic passes ...; print() is documented to return its argument invisibly

summary.book that prints and returns something

summary.book returns a summary.book object with its own print method

R FAQ 8.1

if (class(x) == "book")

inherits(x, "book")

a class vector can have more than one element; length-two conditions are an error since R 4.2.0

Methods in a package left unregistered because exportPattern("^[^.]") exports everything

S3method(generic, class) in NAMESPACE or @export under roxygen2, with the generic imported

a method must be registered to be found when the package is only loaded, not attached

The roxygen2 version recorded in a note-style field of DESCRIPTION

Config/roxygen2/version: (roxygen2 8.x)

roxygen2 8.0.0 moved its settings to Config/roxygen2/*

.S3method() or registerS3method() calls in package code

S3method() in NAMESPACE (or @export with roxygen2); .S3method() in scripts

the help page for .S3method() says it is meant for scripts

foo.default <- base::foo to make a base function generic

foo.default <- function(object, ...) base::foo(object)

the assignment captures the function at install time and goes out of date (Writing R Extensions)

setOldClass() to declare an S3 class

nothing for S3; setOldClass() only when an S3 class must be used in an S4 slot or method signature

it belongs to the S4 system

x$na for x$name on a list-based object

[[ with the full name, options(warnPartialMatchDollar = TRUE) while testing

partial matching returns a wrong value silently

methods(print) to see everything

methods(class = "book") and getS3method()

the generic’s list is very long and shows only what the loaded packages register

Source: Writing R Extensions: Registering S3 methods

The community books Advanced R (the S3 chapter, which also uses the constructor, validator and helper vocabulary) and R Packages cover the same ground in a tutorial style; they are named here as community material and are not part of the official documentation this page derives from. The official manuals are older than both and make a point that the newer material sometimes drops: S3 gives no safety net, and every guarantee is a convention that you have to keep.
